content: The iodine value, also known as the iodine adsorption value or iodine number, is a chemical parameter that quantifies the mass of iodine, in grams, that reacts with 100 grams of a given chemical substance. When iodine is dissolved in a solution, it appears yellow or brown in color. Any reactive chemical groups within the substance that interact with iodine will cause the color to disappear at a specific concentration. The amount of iodine solution required to maintain the yellow or brown color serves as an indicator of the quantity of iodine-sensitive reactive groups present in the substance. One significant application of the iodine number is in determining the degree of unsaturation in fatty acids. This is because double bonds in fatty acids react with iodine compounds. A higher iodine number indicates a greater presence of unsaturated fatty acid bonds within a fat sample. In a standard procedure to measure the iodine value, the fatty acid is treated with an excess of Hanus solution, which is a solution of iodobromine (BrI). Any unreacted iodobromine is then reacted with potassium iodide, which converts it into iodine. The concentration of iodine is subsequently determined through titration with sodium thiosulfate. Standardized methods for this analysis include ASTM D1959-97 and DIN 53241. For example, 2 grams of the fat sample are mixed with 20 cm³ of Wijs solution and 10 cm³ of 1,1,1-trichloroethane. This mixture is left in the dark for 30 minutes. Following this, 15 cm³ of a 10% potassium iodide solution and 10 cm³ of deionized water are added. The iodine concentration is then titrated using a 1 M sodium thiosulfate solution. The difference between a control titration (without the fat sample) and the titration with the fat sample is calculated. This difference, when multiplied by a specific factor, provides the mass of iodine absorbed by the oil.
